paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Σωκράτης ἐν ταῖς Ἀθήναις ἔζη. πολλάκις ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ τοῖς φίλοις διελέγετο. οὐ μόνον περὶ τῆς πόλεως ἔλεγεν, ἀλλὰ καὶ περὶ τοῦ βίου καὶ τῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν.
Σῖτον μὲν ἤσθιεν ὁ Σωκράτης, ποτὸν δὲ ἔπινεν· ὀλίγων δὲ ἐδεῖτο. ἡ γὰρ πεῖνα αὐτῷ τὸν σῖτον ἡδὺν ἐποίει. οὐκ ἀεὶ τὰ πολυτελῆ ἐζήτει.
Οἱ μὲν φίλοι ἔβλεπον τὸν βίον αὐτοῦ, οἱ δὲ τοὺς λόγους ἤκουον. ὁ Σωκράτης οὐ λόγῳ μόνον ἐδίδασκεν· καὶ τῷ ἔργῳ παράδειγμα παρεῖχεν.
Σκέψασθε νῦν τὴν ἐρώτησιν· τίς ἄρξει τῶν φίλων ἐν κινδύνῳ; ὁ τῶν ἐπιθυμιῶν ἥττων ἢ ὁ ἑαυτοῦ κρατῶν; οἱ φίλοι οὐ μόνον ἡδονὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ βοήθειαν ζητοῦσιν.
Ἐν τῷ παραδείγματι ὁ ἀνὴρ ἤσθιεν, ὁ δὲ φίλος ἦλθεν. ὁ ἀνὴρ τὸν φίλον εἶδεν καὶ ἤκουσεν. οὐ πᾶσα χρεία ἔμενεν· ἔργον γὰρ ἦν παρόν.
Ἡ ἐγκράτεια οὐ λόγος μόνον ἐστίν. ὁ μὲν ἀνὴρ περὶ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ἔλεγεν, ὁ δὲ τὸ ἀγαθὸν ἔπραττεν. τίς τῶν δύο τοῖς φίλοις πιστὸς ἦν;

reading.translation:
Socrates lived in Athens. He often conversed with his friends in the marketplace. He spoke not only about the city but also about life and desires.

Socrates ate food and drank drink, but he needed few things. For hunger made his food pleasant to him. He was not always seeking expensive things.

Some friends observed his way of life, while others listened to his words. Socrates did not teach by speech alone; he also provided an example by action.

Consider the question now: who will lead friends in danger? The person weaker than his desires or the person mastering himself? Friends seek not only pleasure but also help.

In the example the man was eating, and his friend arrived. The man saw his friend and listened. Not every need waited; for a task was at hand.

Self-mastery is not merely a word. One man was speaking about the good, while the other was doing good. Which of the two was dependable to his friends?

wordStudy.label: Word Study — ἐγκράτεια: having command of oneself

blocks.title: ἐγκράτεια: having command of oneself
body: ἐγκράτεια names mastery or control. In this lesson it concerns managing desires so that a person can act dependably. The related adjective ἐγκρατής describes someone who has that command.

κρατέω can take a genitive of what is mastered: ἑαυτοῦ κρατεῖ, “he masters himself.” σωφροσύνη is the broader module term, encompassing sound judgment and moderation; the words overlap without being interchangeable in every passage.

sections.title: 1. Building the imperfect active
body: The imperfect indicative presents a past action from within: it was happening, used to happen, or kept happening. Add the augment to the present stem, then secondary endings. A consonant-initial stem takes ἐ-; an initial vowel normally lengthens.
The active endings are -ον, -ες, -ε(ν), -ομεν, -ετε, -ον. First singular and third plural coincide, so find the subject. The imperfect uses the present stem, not the aorist stem.

sections.title: 2. Imperfect middle and deponent verbs
body: Middle and passive imperfects share one set of endings: -όμην, -ου, -ετο, -όμεθα, -εσθε, -οντο. Their meaning depends on the verb and context. A deponent such as διαλέγομαι retains its ordinary sense, “converse.”
Do not call every -ετο form passive. In the reading διελέγετο means “he was conversing”; ἐδεῖτο means “he needed” and takes a genitive. Formal passive analysis becomes a main topic in Lesson 31.

sections.title: 3. Contract verbs and εἰμί in the past
body: Contract verbs retain their contraction rules after augmentation: ἐποίεε becomes ἐποίει, and ἐποίεον becomes ἐποίουν. The latter can mean “I was making” or “they were making.” Identify person from context.
Learn εἰμί separately: ἦν, ἦσθα, ἦν, ἦμεν, ἦτε, ἦσαν. English “was” does not automatically make a Greek form passive; εἰμί simply links a subject with a description.

sections.title: 4. Choosing a viewpoint: imperfect and aorist
body: Imperfect and aorist are both past in the indicative, but they offer different views. ἤσθιεν shows eating in progress; ἦλθεν presents an arrival as a whole. Neither tense tells us by itself how many minutes an event lasted.
A long event can be aorist when summarized; a brief action can be imperfect when pictured in progress or repeated. Use the narrative setting, not the rule “aorist means sudden.”

sections.title: Meet Xenophon’s Memorabilia
body: The Memorabilia is a four-book defense and portrait of Socrates, assembled through conversations, recollections, and examples of conduct. Its traditional English title means “recollections.” Xenophon wants readers to see Socrates as useful to his companions and worthy of respect. That purpose shapes the selection of episodes.

Think of the four books as a gallery of encounters rather than a continuous biography. Book 1 answers accusations against Socrates and presents his religious practice and daily conduct. Books 2–3 explore family, friendship, useful work, and leadership. Book 4 gives sustained attention to education, including the questioning of Euthydemus. The movement from an ordinary habit to a public responsibility is characteristic of the collection.

Xenophon writes as an advocate for a teacher condemned at Athens in 399 BCE. His Socrates improves other people through example, questions, and practical reasoning. That organizing purpose makes the work valuable evidence for an ancient interpretation of Socrates; it does not make every conversation a stenographic record. Notice who asks the questions, who changes position, and where the narrator supplies the judgment.

Reading invitation: open Book 1, chapter 5, then Book 4, chapter 5. Ask whether mastery of appetite is merely a rule about pleasure or a condition for learning and dependable action. Keep a small dossier of the different kinds of evidence Xenophon offers: reported speech, observed habit, analogy, and the narrator’s praise.

This reading joins two passages: ordinary habits in 1.3 and the question of trusting an undisciplined leader in 1.5. It is not a diary entry. Our Greek arranges the material into a typical day and adds a short teaching example; the habits are source-based, but the day’s timetable is reconstructed.

sections.title: The meal as evidence
body: A small cup and an uncomplicated meal become part of an argument about character. Xenophon presents Socrates as enjoying food without needing an elaborate supply of luxuries. The point is freedom from demands that could make him less dependable.

The Reading banner imagines a simple meal; the Culture/History banner moves the question of trust into a marketplace. A grain seller and customers depend on reliable conduct. Both are modern reconstructions, not evidence of a recorded meeting or a particular ancient transaction.

sections.title: Self-command is a social virtue
body: The striking move in 1.5 is from appetite to trust: would you entrust important responsibilities to someone unable to govern himself? Self-control matters because other people depend on the leader’s attention.

That argument deserves examination. Having few possessions is not itself proof of virtue, and needing food is not a failure of character. Compare a chosen restraint with a deprivation someone cannot escape. Xenophon’s exemplary portrait is an argument to assess.

sections.title: Try it: the interrupted meal
body: Imagine a friend arriving while you are eating to report a task that needs help. Identify what you know, what you would need to ask, and what responsibility you have. There need not be one identical decision in every case.

Return to the Greek: ἤσθιεν supplies the ongoing meal; ἦλθεν introduces the arrival. Explain how the two viewpoints make the decision visible. Then give one reason a dependable person might pause the meal and one reason the friend’s request might need clarification.
